subject: Archaeology
title: The First Medical Texts
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The First Medical Texts.

hook.text: Babylonian doctors kept medical records on clay tablets — case notes, prescriptions, and even surgical instructions.

buildup.text: The Diagnostic Handbook from 1000 BCE lists symptoms head-to-toe and gives treatments for each condition.

discovery.text: Many remedies used real medicinal plants — some overlap with modern pharmacology. Others invoked demons and spells.

twist.text: Doctors were legally accountable. Hammurabi's Code said if a surgeon killed a patient with a bronze knife, his hand was cut off.

climax.text: Babylonian medicine combined observation, herbalism, and religion — not so different from medieval European medicine.

punchline.text: They mixed herbs with spells and held surgeons legally accountable.

quiz.question: What legal consequence did Babylonian surgeons face under Hammurabi's Code?
options: They had to pay the patient's family double the medical fee
A surgeon who killed a patient could lose his hand
They were banished from the city for one year

details.summary: Mesopotamian medical tablets from as early as 2100 BCE describe symptoms, diagnoses, and treatments combining practical remedies with magical incantations. These texts reveal a medical system where observation-based treatment coexisted with supernatural explanations for disease.
details.whyItMatters: These texts show that systematic medical thinking is nearly as old as writing. The blend of practical and magical approaches reveals how early societies understood illness before modern germ theory.
takeaways: Medical tablets date from as early as 2100 BCE
They describe symptoms, diagnoses, and treatments in detail
Practical remedies coexisted with magical incantations

faq.question: Did Mesopotamian medicine actually work?
faq.answer: Some treatments were effective — they used antiseptic substances like honey and salt, set broken bones, and performed basic surgery. Other treatments relied on incantations or substances with no medicinal value. Their observation skills were strong even when their explanations were wrong.

faq.question: How did Mesopotamians explain disease?
faq.answer: Disease was often attributed to angry gods, demons, or witchcraft. Doctors diagnosed both the physical condition and its supernatural cause. Treatment addressed both — practical remedies for the body and rituals to appease the spiritual cause simultaneously.
